description: A passionate, innovation-driven team focused on solving real-world challenges through AI, machine learning, data science, and space technology. We aim to transform creative ideas into impactful, scalable solutions using NASA's open data and emerging technologies. We're looking for enthusiastic members skilled in AI/ML, astronomy, astrophysics, GIS, full-stack development, and UI/UX who thrive on collaboration, creativity, and innovation.
summary:
The 3D Hemispherical Sky-Dome View puts a virtual glass dome over the lunar lander, so you can see the whole 360-degree sky in one interactive picture. The flat base shows compass direction (azimuth, 0 to 360 degrees). The curved walls show elevation, from the horizon up to the zenith at 90 degrees. Along the bottom edge, a dark, jagged outline marks the mountains and crater rims around the landing site. It’s built from LOLA topography data, so it shows exactly what terrain blocks the view.

On top of that skyline, the dome traces the Sun’s path around the horizon over the 29.5-day lunar cycle. It also shows Earth’s small oval wobble in the sky, which comes from lunar libration. When the Sun slips behind the skyline, the view flags a solar power shadow. When Earth does, it flags a direct-to-Earth communication blackout.

Mission planners can drag a time slider or switch landing sites and watch the line-of-sight rays move as they do it. That lets them compare operating windows in seconds.
details:
What It Does & How It Works Lunar Landing Site Navigator calculates where the Sun and Earth sit in the sky at a lunar landing site on any chosen date and turns complex ephemeris math into two plain-language answers: Can it make power? and Can it phone home?

Users pick a site (Apollo, Artemis/CLPS candidates, Chang'e-4, or custom coordinates) and a date. Using the astronomy-engine library, the app rotates Moon-to-Sun and Moon-to-Earth vectors into the Moon's body-fixed frame (including lunar libration) and compares them against the local horizon silhouette. Results are displayed across four views:

  • 2D Horizon Panorama: A flat skyline view with exaggerated vertical elevation so sub-7° polar grazing angles are easy to read.
  • 3D Hemispherical Sky-Dome: An interactive 3D dome tracing the Sun’s 29.5-day path and Earth’s libration wobble against local terrain obstacles.
  • 30-Day Timeline & Side-by-Side Comparator: Compares up to three site/date combinations at once and simulates 7-, 14-, or 21-day launch slips.
  • Technical Toggle: Reveals raw azimuths, elevations, solar flux, and exact bisected sunset/Earth set times (to within ~1 minute) for mission planners.

Benefits & Intended Impact Tools like JPL Horizons, Moon Trek, and Quick Map are built for deep analysis, not fast comparison. Our tool lets users evaluate schedule slips or backup sites in seconds without learning coordinate frames. It serves three audiences at once: the public gets clear mission verdicts, educators get an intuitive visual showing why south-pole lighting and Earth visibility are so extreme, and mission planners get a rapid screening aid before moving to heavy GIS tools.

Tools, Languages & Software

  • Frontend & 3D: TypeScript, React 18, Vite, Tailwind CSS, and Three.js, deployed on Vercel.
  • Astrodynamics & Validation: astronomy-engine (IAU rotation model) and Vitest. We validated our math against live NASA JPL Horizons API queries across 12 test cases (Shackleton, Malapert, and Apollo 11 on 1 Jan, 3 Jul, and 15 Nov 2026), matching Horizons to within 0.02°.
  • Development Workflow: We used AI coding assistants (Claude and OpenAI Codex) to help write and review code, while our team defined the architecture, caught and fixed an early Sun-vector frame offset via JPL Horizons testing, and verified all outputs.

How It Is Creative

  • Experience-to-Instrument Flow: A scroll-driven 3D launch-to-landing story transitions directly into the working Sky-Dome at the selected site.
  • Built for Polar Geometry: Exaggerated horizon rendering makes tiny polar elevation angles legible at a glance.
  • Launch-Slip Simulator: Directly solves the real-world challenge of hardware delays by showing how a 1- to 3-week slip changes mission viability.

Factors Our Team Considered

  • Accuracy First: Our initial build had a Sun-position frame error; we caught it by testing against independent calculations and JPL Horizons, fixed the body-fixed transformation, and added multi-date regression tests.
  • Honest Data Labeling: Bundled terrain profiles are explicitly labeled as approximate (with custom horizon upload support), and the app reports explicit "Always Up" or "Never Up" states instead of fake countdowns.
  • Accessibility & Attribution: Built with plain language by default, technical metrics on demand, keyboard navigation, and reduced-motion support. Ephemeris methods rely on astronomy-engine and NASA JPL Horizons.
